=== #812 ===
engine/core: encode-side fail-closed guards for the child read-path rejects
## Context

PR #811 (issue #802) added four decode/verify-side hard rejects on the child read path whose matching produce paths do not exist yet. Per the AGENTS.md encode/decode fail-closed symmetry rule, each producer must land with a release-active `Err` guard (never `debug_assert!`) plus a test that fires in a release build — otherwise a release build can publish bytes its own decoder rejects.

## Debts

When the content-bearing write / child-publish paths land, each of these decode-side rejects needs its encode-side twin:

1. **Grant section on a child envelope** — child adoption rejects any envelope carrying a `grantSection` key (`has_grant_section`, `crates/core/src/seal/envelope.rs`). Child envelope sealing must refuse to attach one.
2. **Kind transplant** — `read_content` rejects when the sealed body kind disagrees with the parent's `ChildRef.kind` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs`). Child-ref authoring must enforce the match.
3. **Version size vs manifest size** — `content::open_content` rejects `manifest.size != version.size` (`crates/engine/src/content/mod.rs`). Today `Version::new` and DAG `assemble` take `size` independently; seal/publish must tie them.
4. **Child-ref `ipnsName` well-formedness** — the read path parses the bytes fail-closed as a canonical base36 IPNS name (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs`); child-ref authoring must emit exactly that form.

## Dependency

Depends on the engine content-bearing write / upload slice (surfaces via #807); blocks none. Related precedent: #794.

Found by the /crypto-privacy-review gate on #811.

A loose idea has arrived — too big for one agent session, and wrapped in fog: the way from here to the **destination** isn't visible yet. Wayfinding is about finding that way, not charging at the destination. This skill charts the way as a **shared map** on the repo's issue tracker, then works its **decision tickets** — questions whose resolution is a decision, not slices of a build to execute — one at a time until the route is clear.

The destination varies per effort, and naming it is the first act of charting — it shapes every ticket. It might be a spec to hand off and iterate on, a decision to lock before planning starts, or a change made in place like a data-structure migration. The map is domain-agnostic — engineering work, course content, whatever fits the shape.

## Plan, don't do

Wayfinder is **planning** by default: each ticket resolves a decision, and the map is done when the way is clear — nothing left to decide before someone goes and does the thing. The pull to just do the work is usually the signal you've reached the edge of the map and it's time to hand off. An effort can override this in its **Notes** — carrying execution into the map itself — but absent that, produce decisions, not deliverables.

## Refer by name

Every map and ticket is an issue, so it has a **name** — its title. In everything the human reads — narration, the map's Decisions-so-far — refer to it by that name, never by a bare id, number, or slug. A wall of `#42, #43, #44` is illegible; names read at a glance. The id and URL don't vanish — a name wraps its link — but they ride *inside* the name, never stand in for it.

## The Map

The map is a single issue on this repo's issue tracker, labelled `wayfinder:map` — the canonical artifact. Its tickets are child issues of the map.

The map is an **index**, not a store. It lists the decisions made and points at the tickets that hold their detail; a decision lives in exactly one place — its ticket — so the map never restates it, only gists it and links.

**Where the map, its child tickets, blocking, and frontier queries physically live is tracker-specific.** The issue tracker should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not. Consult the tracker doc's "Wayfinding operations" section for how _this_ repo expresses them. If no tracker has been provided, default to the local-markdown tracker.

### The map body

The whole map at low resolution, loaded once per session. Open tickets are **not** listed — they are open child issues, found by query.

```markdown
## Destination

<what reaching the end of this map looks like — the spec, decision, or change this effort is finding its way to. One or two lines; every session orients to it before choosing a ticket.>

## Notes

<domain; skills every session should consult; standing preferences for this effort>

## Decisions so far

<!-- the index — one line per closed ticket: enough to judge relevance, then zoom the link for the detail the ticket holds -->

- [<closed ticket title>](link) — <one-line gist of the answer>

## Not yet specified

<!-- see "Fog of war": in-scope fog you can't ticket yet; graduates as the frontier advances -->

## Out of scope

<!-- see "Out of scope": work ruled beyond the destination; closed, never graduates -->
```

### Tickets

Each ticket is a **child issue** of the map; the tracker's issue id is its identity. Its body is the question, sized to one 100K token agent session:

```markdown
## Question

<the decision or investigation this ticket resolves>
```

Each ticket carries a `wayfinder:<type>` label — one of `research`, `prototype`, `grilling`, `task` (see [Ticket Types](#ticket-types)).

A session **claims** a ticket by assigning it to the dev driving the map, **first**, before any work, so concurrent sessions skip it. That assignee _is_ the claim: an open, unassigned ticket is unclaimed.

Blocking uses the tracker's **native** dependency relationship — essential because it renders the frontier _visually_ in the tracker's own UI, so the human sees what's takeable without opening the map. Only a tracker that lacks native blocking falls back to a body convention. A ticket is **unblocked** when every ticket blocking it is closed; the **frontier** is the open, unblocked, unclaimed children — the edge of the known.

The answer isn't part of the body — it's recorded on resolution (see [Work through the map](#work-through-the-map)). Assets created while resolving a ticket are linked from the issue, not pasted in.

## Ticket Types

Every ticket is either **HITL** — human in the loop, worked *with* a human who speaks for themselves — or **AFK**, driven by the agent alone. A HITL ticket only resolves through that live exchange; the agent never stands in for the human's side of it (a grilling agent that answers its own questions has broken this).

- **Research** (AFK): Reading documentation, third-party APIs, or local resources like knowledge bases to surface a fact a decision waits on. Resolved by a `/research` **subagent**. Use when knowledge outside the current working directory is required.
- **Prototype** (HITL): Raise the fidelity of the discussion by making a cheap, rough, concrete artifact to react to — an outline, a rough take, a stub, or UI/logic code via the /prototype skill. Links the prototype as an asset. Use when "how should it look" or "how should it behave" is the key question.
- **Grilling** (HITL): Conversation via the /grilling and /domain-modeling skills, one question at a time. The default case.
- **Task** (HITL or AFK): Manual work that must happen before a *decision* can be made — nothing to decide, prototype, or research, but the discussion is blocked until it's done. Signing up for a service so its API can be judged, provisioning access, moving data so its shape can be seen. This is the one type that *does* rather than decides — and it earns its place by unblocking a decision, not by delivering the destination. The agent drives it alone where it can (AFK); otherwise it hands the human a precise checklist (HITL). Resolved when the work is done; the answer records what was done and any resulting facts (credentials location, new URLs, row counts) later tickets depend on.

## Fog of war

The map is _deliberately_ incomplete: don't chart what you can't yet see. Beyond the live tickets lies the **fog of war** — the dim view of decisions and investigations you can tell are coming but can't yet pin down, because they hang on questions still open. Resolving a ticket clears the fog ahead of it, graduating whatever's now specifiable into fresh tickets — one at a time, until the way to the destination is clear and no tickets remain.

The map's **Not yet specified** section is where that dim view is written down: the suspected question, the area to revisit later. It's the undiscovered frontier _toward_ the destination — everything here is in scope, just not sharp enough to ticket. Write as loosely or as fully as the view allows; it doubles as a signpost for collaborators reading where the effort is headed.

**Fog or ticket?** The test is whether you can state the question precisely now — _not_ whether you can answer it now.

- **Ticket when** the question is already sharp — even if it's blocked and you can't act on it yet.
- **Not yet specified when** you can't yet phrase it that sharply. Don't pre-slice the fog into ticket-sized pieces: it's coarser than a ticket, and one patch may graduate into several tickets, or none, once the frontier reaches it.

**Not yet specified** excludes what's already decided (Decisions so far), what's already a live ticket, and what's out of scope (the next section).

## Out of scope

Fog only ever gathers _toward_ the destination. The destination fixes the scope, so work beyond it is **out of scope** — it isn't fog, and it doesn't belong in **Not yet specified**. It gets its own **Out of scope** section on the map: work you've consciously ruled out of _this_ effort. Scope, not sharpness, lands it here.

Out-of-scope work never graduates — the frontier stops at the destination — so it returns only if the destination is redrawn, and then as a fresh effort, not a resumption.

Ruling something out of scope is a scoping act, not a step on the route. When a ticket that already exists turns out to sit past the destination — mis-scoped in while charting, or exposed by a resolution — **close it** (a closed ticket is unambiguously off the frontier) and leave one line in the **Out of scope** section: the gist plus why it's out of scope, linking the closed ticket. It stays out of **Decisions so far**, which records the route actually walked — a scope boundary isn't a step on it.

## Invocation

Two modes. Either way, **never resolve more than one ticket per session** — with the exception of research tickets.

### Chart the map

User invokes with a loose idea.

1. **Name the destination.** Run a `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` session to pin down what this map is finding its way to — the spec, decision, or change. The destination fixes the scope, so it's settled first.
2. **Map the frontier.** Grill again, **breadth-first** this time: fan out across the whole space rather than deep on any one thread, surfacing the open decisions and the first steps takeable now. **If this surfaces no fog** — the way to the destination is already clear, the whole journey small enough for one session — you don't need a map. Stop and ask the user how they'd like to proceed.
3. **Create the map** (label `wayfinder:map`): Destination and Notes filled in, Decisions-so-far empty, the fog sketched into **Not yet specified**.
4. **Create the tickets you can specify now** as child issues of the map — then wire blocking edges in a **second pass** (issues need ids before they can reference each other). Wiring sorts them into the frontier and the blocked; everything you can't yet specify stays in the fog — the **Not yet specified** section.
5. **Fire the research subagents.** For each `research` ticket you just created, spin up a `/research` subagent to resolve it in parallel, capturing its findings on a throwaway `research/<name>` branch with a context pointer from the ticket.
6. Stop — charting is one session's work; it hand-resolves nothing.

### Work through the map

User invokes with a map (URL or number). A ticket is **optional** — without one, you pick the next decision, not the user.

1. Load the **map** — the low-res view, not every ticket body.
2. Choose the ticket. If the user named one, use it. Otherwise take the first frontier ticket in order. **Claim it**: assign it to yourself before any work.
3. Resolve it — **zoom as needed**: fetch the full body of any related or closed ticket on demand; invoke the skills the `## Notes` block names. If in doubt, use `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling`.
4. Record the resolution: post the answer as a **resolution comment**, **close** the issue, and **append a context pointer** to the map's Decisions-so-far.
5. Add newly-surfaced tickets (create-then-wire); graduate any fog the answer has made specifiable, clearing each graduated patch from **Not yet specified** so it lives only as its new ticket. If the answer reveals a ticket — this one or another — sits beyond the destination, **rule it out of scope** rather than resolving it on the route. If the decision invalidates other parts of the map, update or delete those tickets.

The user may run unblocked tickets in parallel, so expect other sessions to be editing the tracker concurrently.

Part of #813

## Question

Where does the upload boundary sit relative to the durable op journal — does `Engine::command` seal and stage, with upload deferred to the drain driver, or does it seal and upload eagerly and journal only the resulting CIDs?

This is the load-bearing decision of the map: the drain driver's shape, content key custody, cancel semantics, and the pending-overlay projection all follow from it.

## What is fixed already

`blueprint/engine.md:208-211` and `web-client.md:189-193` are unambiguous that a content write is **one journaled op regardless of online state**, and the op model already carries the seam: `OpKind::Create { content_staging_key: Option<Vec<u8>> }` and `OpKind::UpdateContent { content_staging_key: Vec<u8> }` (`crates/engine/src/sync/op.rs:37-82`). No bytes and no CIDs ride an op by design (`op.rs:11-13`). `stage_op(store, profile, op, upload: Option<&[u8]>)` (`sync/staging.rs:47-83`) already writes staged bytes **before** enqueuing the op, and `staging.rs:40-42` guarantees no plaintext user content lands in the staging store at rest.

So the fork is not *whether* it goes through the queue — it is *when the bytes leave the device*.

## Candidates

1. **Seal at command time, upload at drain.** Blueprint-aligned, offline-correct. Requires the per-version content key to survive the durable boundary (see the blocked custody ticket) and requires the drain driver to own the upload retry.
2. **Seal and upload at command time, journal the CIDs.** Simpler key handling — the key never outlives the call. Breaks offline parity: a queued op could never be created offline.
3. **Hybrid — upload at command time when online, at drain when offline.** Two code paths for the same op; likely the worst of both, but should be considered and rejected explicitly rather than by omission.

## Notes for the resolving session

`stage_and_notify` (`facade.rs:1581-1597`) currently hardcodes `upload = None` and maps `StageOutcome::RejectedOverBudget` onto an internal `EngineError::Seam`. There is no `EngineError::OverBudget` variant (`facade.rs:449-512`), so the blueprint's law that "only new uploads fail fast past the budget; metadata ops queue unbounded" (`engine.md:233-235`) is currently unexpressible — whichever candidate wins, that error surface needs designing here.

## Question

After a successful publish, does the write path seed the base snapshot and cache, or does the user eat a full resolve plus gateway round trip for bytes the device just held?

## Why it is a fork

3. **Do nothing** and accept the latency, on the grounds that the resolve is correct and the cost is a one-time round trip.

## Question

Where does the per-version content key live between `Engine::command` and publish, and what is the crash-recovery story for a staged-but-unpublished version?

## Why it is a fork with a security edge

A content key is a stated **KDF non-edge** — random per version, never derived (`crates/core/src/kdf/mod.rs:18-20`, `core.md:197-198`, `CONTEXT.md:10`). It is minted from raw entropy at `content/chunk.rs:31-35` and is `ZeroizeOnDrop`. So it **cannot be recovered** — if it is lost between sealing and publishing, the staged bytes are permanently unopenable garbage.

If the upload boundary lands after the durable journal, something must carry that key across the boundary. Every option has a cost:

1. **It rides the `Op`.** The op codec is serde_json (`sync/op.rs:178-187`), so this puts a bare symmetric content key in plaintext in the durable op queue. Arguably worse than the plaintext content that `sync/staging.rs:40-42` explicitly forbids at rest.
2. **It goes into the `StagingStore` alongside the sealed bytes.** Same at-rest exposure, different drawer — but at least colocated with what it opens, and covered by the staging budget and GC.
3. **It is held in memory only.** No at-rest exposure; a crash between command and publish orphans the staged bytes with no way to recover the version. Needs a GC story (`orphan_staging_keys`, `staging.rs:88-111`) and an answer for what the user sees.
4. **Seal late** — journal the plaintext-free intent, mint the key at drain. Changes what "staged bytes" means and may collapse into the eager-upload candidate.

## What resolving looks like

Pick where the key lives, state the at-rest exposure that choice accepts, and define the crash-recovery behaviour: what happens to staged bytes whose key is gone, who GCs them, and what the user is told. Confirm the terminal-owner zeroization rule (AGENTS.md rule 7) still holds across whatever boundary is chosen.

## Question

What is the exact ordering of upload, register, and publish — and what is the rollback when a step fails partway?

## Why it is a fork

Blocks must be uploaded and pinned before a record is published, or the read path resolves a valid record pointing at unfetchable CIDs. But **register-first** (`CONTEXT.md:71`, `blueprint/engine.md:464-470` — "register-first ordering is built into the publish pipeline, not left to callers") says the name and CID batch registers before first publish. Meanwhile the upload endpoint creates its own pin row. The CIDs are known locally before any bytes move, because `compute_cid` is a local computation (`crates/core/src/content/cid.rs:70`) — so more orderings are available than are obviously correct.

## Candidates

1. `upload(leaves) -> upload(root) -> upload(envelope) -> register(name, contentCids) -> publish`
2. `register(name, contentCids) -> upload -> publish` — true register-first, viable because CIDs are computable before upload
3. Upload-only, letting the upload endpoint's own pin row satisfy inventory — skips name registration and violates register-first, but should be rejected explicitly

## The rollback half

If publish fails after upload, blocks are pinned and quota-charged with nothing referencing them. Decide which applies:

- GC via `retire` (`net/retire.rs:24`, live today)
- the "registered-never-published orphan, alert-GC'd" residual (`CONTEXT.md:71`)
- retry from the still-queued op, since the op has not been removed

Also decide the symmetric case: register succeeded, upload failed. And what the op queue does in each — retry, dead-letter with bytes preserved (`engine.md:231-235`), or drop.

## Existing machinery

`net::publish::publish` (`net/publish.rs:115`) already implements register-first, floor-plus-one CAS, fanout PUT, and confirm-by-re-resolve — but is only ever called by liveness (`net/liveness.rs:28`) and revival (`net/revival.rs:15`). `PublishRequest.content_cids` (`net/publish.rs:38-53`) exists and every production producer passes an empty vec (`facade.rs:1162` — that is #797).

A new child also needs first-publish-at-sequence-1 semantics (`core.md:207`) plus the parent folder record republished with the new child ref.

## Question

Which layer owns #812's four encode-side fail-closed guards — `crates/core`'s seal API, or the engine's record-authoring layer?

## Why it is a fork

AGENTS.md rule 8 requires every decode-side hard reject to have a matching **release-active** `Err` on the produce path — never `debug_assert!`. #812 lists four such debts, each explicitly waiting on the write plane:

1. **Grant section on a child envelope** — child adoption rejects any envelope carrying a `grantSection` key (`has_grant_section`, `crates/core/src/seal/envelope.rs`); child envelope sealing must refuse to attach one.
2. **Kind transplant** — `read_content` rejects a sealed body kind disagreeing with the parent's `ChildRef.kind` (`facade.rs:1498-1504`); child-ref authoring must enforce the match.
3. **Version size versus manifest size** — `open_content` rejects `manifest.size != version.size` (`content/mod.rs:169-175`). Today `Version::new` (`crates/core/src/seal/body.rs:156-169`) and `dag::assemble` take `size` independently; seal and publish must tie them.
4. **Child-ref `ipnsName` well-formedness** — the read path parses canonical base36 fail-closed (`facade.rs:1434-1441`); authoring must emit exactly that form.

Guard 3 is the clearest illustration of the fork. Enforcing it in **core** means changing `Version::new` to take something `SealedContent`-derived, which touches a frozen encoding and the KAT manifest — but makes the invariant structural and unbypassable. Enforcing it in the **engine** is a release-active check at the authoring call site — cheaper, but the guarantee is per-callsite and a future second caller can miss it. Guards 1 and 4 sit at the same choice.

## What resolving looks like

Decide per guard (they need not all land in the same layer), and say for each whether it is structural (the wrong state is unrepresentable) or checked (the wrong state returns `Err`). Every guard needs a test that fires in a **release** build — state how, following the `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs` `assert_children_unique` convention.

Related precedent: #794 (core encode-side recursion depth bound is `debug_assert`-only, unbounded in release) is the same rule-8 class and is still open.

Here's the full detail.

**Leaf sizing is exactly determined.** `seal_chunk` emits `nonce(24) || ciphertext || tag(16)` (`chunk.rs:65`, `aead.rs:15,17`), and ciphertext length equals plaintext length for XChaCha20-Poly1305. So:

```
sealed_leaf_len(i) = plaintext_chunk_len(i) + 40
leaf i < n-1  →  chunkSize + 40
leaf n-1      →  size - chunkSize*(n-1) + 40
empty file    →  size 0, exactly 1 leaf, 40 bytes   (chunk.rs:84-86)
n = expected_leaf_count(size, chunkSize) = ceil(size/chunkSize), or 1 when size==0   (dag.rs:207-213)
```

**The root block already carries everything needed to reconstruct that.** `decode_root` returns `{chunk_size, size, leaf_cids}` (`dag.rs:143-150`) and validates on the way through: nonzero chunk size, every link a well-formed `raw` content CID, and `links.len() == expected_leaf_count(size, chunkSize)` (`dag.rs:178-192`). So given the root block plus a concatenated leaf stream, leaf boundaries are recoverable with no additional metadata, and each parsed leaf can be checked with `compute_cid(0x55, leaf) == links[i]` — a fail-closed integrity check on the staged blob for free.

**A correction to what I said earlier, because it changes the comparison:** I called a serialized `SealedContent` "a new wire format," implying novelty was the cost. The real cost is worse and more specific. `Op` uses `serde_json` (`op.rs:181`), so serde is the established internal precedent — but `serde_json` encodes `Vec<u8>` as a JSON array of decimal numbers, roughly **4x inflation**. Harmless for a small `Op`; for multi-MB sealed content it would quadruple staged bytes and corrupt the `staged_bytes_total` budget accounting that `stage_op` gates on. So "follow the `Op` precedent" is actively the wrong move here.

Using core's det-CBOR instead avoids the inflation (CBOR byte strings are length-prefixed raw), but `encode` builds a `Value` tree (`dag.rs:116-124`) — for a multi-MB file that means materializing the whole payload as `Value::Bytes` nodes before encoding, on top of the copies `#815` is already worried about.

**One more fact that matters downstream:** `ApiClient::upload` takes one blob and returns one `UploadResult { cid, size }` (`api/client.rs:292-303`, `types.rs:197-202`). So a drain uploads **N+1 times** — every leaf, plus the root. The staged blob must therefore yield per-block byte ranges at drain regardless of which option you pick; that is not an argument between them, it's a constraint on all of them.

Storage overhead of keeping leaf CIDs explicitly, for reference: 36 bytes per leaf, so ~0.003% at a 1 MiB chunk size. Negligible either way — this decision is about robustness and memory, not size.

## Question

`SealedContent` is a DAG root block plus N sealed leaf blocks, but the staging store holds **one opaque blob under one key** (`seams/staging_store.rs:38`) and an `Op` carries exactly **one** `content_staging_key` (`sync/op.rs:46`, `:81`). What reconciles the two?

Surfaced while resolving #814. Blocked by #815, because every axis that separates the candidates — peak memory, whether the whole payload is held at once, whether upload is chunk-at-a-time — is what the memory model decides.

## Established facts

Leaf sizing is exactly determined. `seal_chunk` emits `nonce(24) || ciphertext || tag(16)` (`content/chunk.rs:65`, `core/src/suite/aead.rs:15,17`) and ciphertext length equals plaintext length, so:

```
sealed_leaf_len(i) = plaintext_chunk_len(i) + 40
leaf i < n-1  ->  chunkSize + 40
leaf n-1      ->  size - chunkSize*(n-1) + 40
empty file    ->  size 0, exactly one leaf, 40 bytes     (chunk.rs:84-86)
n = ceil(size / chunkSize), or 1 when size == 0          (dag.rs:207-213)
```

The root block already carries what is needed to reconstruct that: `decode_root` returns `{chunk_size, size, leaf_cids}` and validates nonzero chunk size, well-formed `raw` leaf CIDs, and `links.len() == expected_leaf_count` (`dag.rs:159-199`). Leaf CIDs are derivable, not independent data — `compute_cid(CONTENT_CID_CODEC, sealed)` (`chunk.rs:94`).

A drain uploads **N+1 times**: `ApiClient::upload` takes one blob and returns one `UploadResult { cid, size }` (`api/client.rs:292-303`). Every candidate must therefore yield per-block byte ranges at drain; that is a shared constraint, not a differentiator.

Note `serde_json` — the existing internal `Op` encoding (`op.rs:181`) — is **not** a viable precedent here: it encodes `Vec<u8>` as a JSON array of decimals, roughly 4x inflation, which would quadruple staged bytes and corrupt the `staged_bytes_total` budget accounting `stage_op` gates on.

## Candidates

Let S = total sealed bytes, n = leaf count.

| | A: root + concat leaves | B: concat leaves only | C: det-CBOR SealedContent | D: key per block |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Peak mem, seal | ~2S | ~2S | ~3S | ~S + chunk |
| Peak mem, drain | ~S + chunk | ~S + chunk | ~3S | ~chunk |
| Boundary recovery | own root manifest | ambient `ContentProfile` | explicit | n/a |
| Survives chunk-size change | yes | **no** | yes | yes |
| Self-integrity check | per-leaf CID | **none** | per-leaf CID | per-leaf CID |
| Resumable upload | no | no | no | **yes** |
| New code | u32 framing + parser | solver for n | codec mapping + versioning | rework 2 landed fns |

**A — root block + concatenated leaves.** `[u32 root_len][root_block][leaf_0]...[leaf_n-1]`. Boundary recovery and per-leaf CID verification come free from an already-frozen, already-validated artifact. Wants a version byte on the outer framing eventually.

**B — concatenated leaves only.** `size` is absent from the blob, so `n` and the last-leaf length must be solved from `blob_len` and the ambient chunk size. **Candidate 1: seal at command time, stage the sealed bytes, upload at drain.**

This is ratified rather than freshly chosen — the landed code already binds it in contract text, and the ticket's three-way framing was wrong to treat it as open:

- `sync/op.rs:11-13` — "Content bytes never live in an op … the bytes sit in the staging store behind the profile budget."
- The staging budget (`SyncTimingProfile::staging_budget_bytes`, enforced at `staging.rs:54-70`) exists specifically so an **offline** device can stage an upload, which only has meaning if upload is deferred past the journal.

Candidate 2 (seal and upload eagerly, journal CIDs) is excluded: it would break the offline parity `blueprint/engine.md:208-211` and `web-client.md:189-193` require — "one journaled op regardless of online state". Candidate 3 (hybrid, upload eagerly when online) collapses with it and is rejected explicitly: two code paths for one op, with no offline guarantee bought.

## Consequences to carry into the slice chain

**The over-budget error surface must be designed with the command.** `stage_and_notify` (`facade.rs:1581-1597`) currently hardcodes `upload = None` and maps `StageOutcome::RejectedOverBudget` onto an internal `EngineError::Seam`. There is no `EngineError::OverBudget` variant (`facade.rs:449-512`), so the law that "past the budget only new uploads fail fast, while metadata ops queue unbounded" (`engine.md:233-235`, restated at `staging.rs:5-9`) is currently unexpressible at the facade boundary. A content-bearing `Create`/`UpdateContent` needs a typed over-budget error carrying `{staged, incoming, budget}`, distinct from a seam failure.

**A drain uploads N+1 times.** `ApiClient::upload` takes one blob and returns one `UploadResult { cid, size }` (`api/client.rs:292-303`), so every leaf plus the root is a separate call. This is an input to the ordering-and-rollback question (#819): a partial upload is the common case, not an edge case.

## Newly surfaced

Establishing the above exposed a sharper question the ticket did not anticipate: `SealedContent` is a root block plus N leaf blocks, but the staging store holds one opaque blob under one key and an `Op` carries exactly one `content_staging_key`. Filed as #828 with the full candidate comparison, blocked by #815 — the memory model determines the answer, so deciding the blob shape first would prejudge it from the wrong end.

## Still open, deliberately

Where the per-version content key lives across the durable boundary is **not** answered here — that is #818, which this ticket unblocks. Candidate 1 is what makes it hard: the key is a KDF non-edge (`crates/core/src/kdf/mod.rs:18-20`), so it cannot be re-derived, and something must carry it from command to drain.

A loose idea has arrived — too big for one agent session, and wrapped in fog: the way from here to the **destination** isn't visible yet. Wayfinding is about finding that way, not charging at the destination. This skill charts the way as a **shared map** on the repo's issue tracker, then works its **decision tickets** — questions whose resolution is a decision, not slices of a build to execute — one at a time until the route is clear.

The destination varies per effort, and naming it is the first act of charting — it shapes every ticket. It might be a spec to hand off and iterate on, a decision to lock before planning starts, or a change made in place like a data-structure migration. The map is domain-agnostic — engineering work, course content, whatever fits the shape.

## Plan, don't do

Wayfinder is **planning** by default: each ticket resolves a decision, and the map is done when the way is clear — nothing left to decide before someone goes and does the thing. The pull to just do the work is usually the signal you've reached the edge of the map and it's time to hand off. An effort can override this in its **Notes** — carrying execution into the map itself — but absent that, produce decisions, not deliverables.

## Refer by name

Every map and ticket is an issue, so it has a **name** — its title. In everything the human reads — narration, the map's Decisions-so-far — refer to it by that name, never by a bare id, number, or slug. A wall of `#42, #43, #44` is illegible; names read at a glance. The id and URL don't vanish — a name wraps its link — but they ride *inside* the name, never stand in for it.

## The Map

The map is a single issue on this repo's issue tracker, labelled `wayfinder:map` — the canonical artifact. Its tickets are child issues of the map.

The map is an **index**, not a store. It lists the decisions made and points at the tickets that hold their detail; a decision lives in exactly one place — its ticket — so the map never restates it, only gists it and links.

**Where the map, its child tickets, blocking, and frontier queries physically live is tracker-specific.** The issue tracker should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not. Consult the tracker doc's "Wayfinding operations" section for how _this_ repo expresses them. If no tracker has been provided, default to the local-markdown tracker.

### The map body

The whole map at low resolution, loaded once per session. Open tickets are **not** listed — they are open child issues, found by query.

```markdown
## Destination

<what reaching the end of this map looks like — the spec, decision, or change this effort is finding its way to. One or two lines; every session orients to it before choosing a ticket.>

## Notes

<domain; skills every session should consult; standing preferences for this effort>

## Decisions so far

<!-- the index — one line per closed ticket: enough to judge relevance, then zoom the link for the detail the ticket holds -->

- [<closed ticket title>](link) — <one-line gist of the answer>

## Not yet specified

<!-- see "Fog of war": in-scope fog you can't ticket yet; graduates as the frontier advances -->

## Out of scope

<!-- see "Out of scope": work ruled beyond the destination; closed, never graduates -->
```

### Tickets

Each ticket is a **child issue** of the map; the tracker's issue id is its identity. Its body is the question, sized to one 100K token agent session:

```markdown
## Question

<the decision or investigation this ticket resolves>
```

Each ticket carries a `wayfinder:<type>` label — one of `research`, `prototype`, `grilling`, `task` (see [Ticket Types](#ticket-types)).

A session **claims** a ticket by assigning it to the dev driving the map, **first**, before any work, so concurrent sessions skip it. That assignee _is_ the claim: an open, unassigned ticket is unclaimed.

Blocking uses the tracker's **native** dependency relationship — essential because it renders the frontier _visually_ in the tracker's own UI, so the human sees what's takeable without opening the map. Only a tracker that lacks native blocking falls back to a body convention. A ticket is **unblocked** when every ticket blocking it is closed; the **frontier** is the open, unblocked, unclaimed children — the edge of the known.

The answer isn't part of the body — it's recorded on resolution (see [Work through the map](#work-through-the-map)). Assets created while resolving a ticket are linked from the issue, not pasted in.

## Ticket Types

Every ticket is either **HITL** — human in the loop, worked *with* a human who speaks for themselves — or **AFK**, driven by the agent alone. A HITL ticket only resolves through that live exchange; the agent never stands in for the human's side of it (a grilling agent that answers its own questions has broken this).

- **Research** (AFK): Reading documentation, third-party APIs, or local resources like knowledge bases to surface a fact a decision waits on. Resolved by a `/research` **subagent**. Use when knowledge outside the current working directory is required.
- **Prototype** (HITL): Raise the fidelity of the discussion by making a cheap, rough, concrete artifact to react to — an outline, a rough take, a stub, or UI/logic code via the /prototype skill. Links the prototype as an asset. Use when "how should it look" or "how should it behave" is the key question.
- **Grilling** (HITL): Conversation via the /grilling and /domain-modeling skills, one question at a time. The default case.
- **Task** (HITL or AFK): Manual work that must happen before a *decision* can be made — nothing to decide, prototype, or research, but the discussion is blocked until it's done. Signing up for a service so its API can be judged, provisioning access, moving data so its shape can be seen. This is the one type that *does* rather than decides — and it earns its place by unblocking a decision, not by delivering the destination. The agent drives it alone where it can (AFK); otherwise it hands the human a precise checklist (HITL). Resolved when the work is done; the answer records what was done and any resulting facts (credentials location, new URLs, row counts) later tickets depend on.

## Fog of war

The map is _deliberately_ incomplete: don't chart what you can't yet see. Beyond the live tickets lies the **fog of war** — the dim view of decisions and investigations you can tell are coming but can't yet pin down, because they hang on questions still open. Resolving a ticket clears the fog ahead of it, graduating whatever's now specifiable into fresh tickets — one at a time, until the way to the destination is clear and no tickets remain.

The map's **Not yet specified** section is where that dim view is written down: the suspected question, the area to revisit later. It's the undiscovered frontier _toward_ the destination — everything here is in scope, just not sharp enough to ticket. Write as loosely or as fully as the view allows; it doubles as a signpost for collaborators reading where the effort is headed.

**Fog or ticket?** The test is whether you can state the question precisely now — _not_ whether you can answer it now.

- **Ticket when** the question is already sharp — even if it's blocked and you can't act on it yet.
- **Not yet specified when** you can't yet phrase it that sharply. Don't pre-slice the fog into ticket-sized pieces: it's coarser than a ticket, and one patch may graduate into several tickets, or none, once the frontier reaches it.

**Not yet specified** excludes what's already decided (Decisions so far), what's already a live ticket, and what's out of scope (the next section).

## Out of scope

Fog only ever gathers _toward_ the destination. The destination fixes the scope, so work beyond it is **out of scope** — it isn't fog, and it doesn't belong in **Not yet specified**. It gets its own **Out of scope** section on the map: work you've consciously ruled out of _this_ effort. Scope, not sharpness, lands it here.

Out-of-scope work never graduates — the frontier stops at the destination — so it returns only if the destination is redrawn, and then as a fresh effort, not a resumption.

Ruling something out of scope is a scoping act, not a step on the route. When a ticket that already exists turns out to sit past the destination — mis-scoped in while charting, or exposed by a resolution — **close it** (a closed ticket is unambiguously off the frontier) and leave one line in the **Out of scope** section: the gist plus why it's out of scope, linking the closed ticket. It stays out of **Decisions so far**, which records the route actually walked — a scope boundary isn't a step on it.

## Invocation

Two modes. Either way, **never resolve more than one ticket per session** — with the exception of research tickets.

### Chart the map

User invokes with a loose idea.

1. **Name the destination.** Run a `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` session to pin down what this map is finding its way to — the spec, decision, or change. The destination fixes the scope, so it's settled first.
2. **Map the frontier.** Grill again, **breadth-first** this time: fan out across the whole space rather than deep on any one thread, surfacing the open decisions and the first steps takeable now. **If this surfaces no fog** — the way to the destination is already clear, the whole journey small enough for one session — you don't need a map. Stop and ask the user how they'd like to proceed.
3. **Create the map** (label `wayfinder:map`): Destination and Notes filled in, Decisions-so-far empty, the fog sketched into **Not yet specified**.
4. **Create the tickets you can specify now** as child issues of the map — then wire blocking edges in a **second pass** (issues need ids before they can reference each other). Wiring sorts them into the frontier and the blocked; everything you can't yet specify stays in the fog — the **Not yet specified** section.
5. **Fire the research subagents.** For each `research` ticket you just created, spin up a `/research` subagent to resolve it in parallel, capturing its findings on a throwaway `research/<name>` branch with a context pointer from the ticket.
6. Stop — charting is one session's work; it hand-resolves nothing.

### Work through the map

User invokes with a map (URL or number). A ticket is **optional** — without one, you pick the next decision, not the user.

1. Load the **map** — the low-res view, not every ticket body.
2. Choose the ticket. If the user named one, use it. Otherwise take the first frontier ticket in order. **Claim it**: assign it to yourself before any work.
3. Resolve it — **zoom as needed**: fetch the full body of any related or closed ticket on demand; invoke the skills the `## Notes` block names. If in doubt, use `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling`.
4. Record the resolution: post the answer as a **resolution comment**, **close** the issue, and **append a context pointer** to the map's Decisions-so-far.
5. Add newly-surfaced tickets (create-then-wire); graduate any fog the answer has made specifiable, clearing each graduated patch from **Not yet specified** so it lives only as its new ticket. If the answer reveals a ticket — this one or another — sits beyond the destination, **rule it out of scope** rather than resolving it on the route. If the decision invalidates other parts of the map, update or delete those tickets.

The user may run unblocked tickets in parallel, so expect other sessions to be editing the tracker concurrently.

content.text:
Facts established, and two of them correct the ticket's own framing:

**The API's 100 MiB cap is per *block*, not per file.** `ApiClient::upload` uploads one block per call (`client.rs:292`), and `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` gates a single raw request body (`app-setup.ts:8`). So it caps chunk size, which any sane value satisfies — it does not bound file size at all. The real file ceiling is the flat-DAG root cap (~108 GiB at 1 MiB chunks) and client memory.

**The copy amplification is per block, not per file.** `upload` does `content.to_vec()` (`client.rs:298`) and `request_authed` does `body.clone()` to keep a copy for the 401 retry (`client.rs:438-441`) — so ~3x, but of one *block*, bounded by chunk size. The ticket describes this as 3x of a 100 MiB payload; that's only true if the whole file went as one blob, which it doesn't.

Which means **option 3 in the ticket — giving the `Http` seam a streaming body — buys almost nothing.** The HTTP bodies are already chunk-sized. The memory problem is upstream of the wire, in the seal step.

Here's the actual peak, for a file of P bytes:

```
JS heap:    P            (File -> ArrayBuffer)
wasm heap:  P            (wasm_bindgen copies Vec<u8> in — lib.rs:401)
          + P + 40n      (frame_and_seal leaves; plaintext still alive)
          + S            (staged blob assembly, shape per #828)
```

roughly **4P** at peak. On wasm32 that lands against a 4 GiB address space with browsers OOMing well below it — and wasm linear memory does not shrink, so one large upload permanently inflates the worker's footprint for the session.

That reframes the fork. It isn't really "where does streaming go" — it's **does the whole plaintext ever exist in the wasm heap at once**, which surfaces a fourth option the ticket didn't list:

content.text:
Noted — client slices and feeds chunks. That keeps the plaintext in the JS heap where the `File` already lives and never materializes it in wasm, without inventing a pull seam. It does leave two things to settle, and this is the sharper one.

The tension I flagged is resolvable: the engine can still **own** framing policy (the chunk size, per `engine.md:483-487`) while the client does the mechanical slicing — the engine tells the client what size to slice at. That's a policy/mechanism split, not a violation.

What doesn't resolve itself is journaling. `stage_op` is fail-closed on exactly this: a content op carrying a staging key with no bytes is "a broken caller contract" that must never journal (`staging.rs:71-76`). A multi-call push means there's a window where chunks exist but the op doesn't — or worse, the reverse.

questions.question: With the client pushing chunks across multiple calls, when is the op journaled?

options.label: Stage-then-commit
options.description: Client opens a write, pushes chunks (engine seals and stages each as it arrives), then calls commit — and only then is the single op journaled, atomically, referencing already-complete staged bytes. Preserves stage_op's fail-closed invariant untouched and keeps 'one journaled op'. A crash mid-push leaves staged bytes with no op, which orphan_staging_keys already GCs by construction. Recommended.

beginWrite(node) -> WriteHandle { chunkSize }
pushChunk(handle, bytes)      // seal + stage, repeat
commitWrite(handle)           // ONE op journaled here

crash mid-push -> staged bytes, no op -> orphan GC
stage_op invariant (staging.rs:71-76) unchanged

options.label: Journal first, append after
options.description: Op is journaled up front, chunks appended to its staging key as they arrive. Means a durable op can reference incomplete content, which is exactly what staging.rs:71-76 fails closed on today — that invariant would have to be relaxed, and a crash mid-push leaves a queued op pointing at a truncated version.

options.label: One call, client pre-slices
options.description: Client slices but still hands the whole array of chunks in a single facade call. No protocol change and no window at all — but every chunk crosses into wasm at once, which reintroduces the O(P) heap cost the choice was meant to avoid.
